K-ellipticity and discrete B-B condition are listed as conditions to be proved; typed as definitions of the named conditions (claim would also fit) since Theorem 4.1 asserts them.
Displays are written with argument macros (\an{...}, \e{...}) and no closing period, so the sentence-boundary check warns at these prose node edges although they are at sentence boundaries.
The proof of Theorem 4.2 has four moves separated only by displays without periods; the finishing step counts it as at most two sentences and rejects steps, so it has zero steps.
The argument for Theorem 5.1 is the prose paragraph before the theorem; taken as its proof up to 'A summary of these results leads to the error estimates in the following theorem.'

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: We assume that all degrees of freedom vanish and show that $\tau=0$. Note that the mean moment becomes the value of $\tau$ for a $0$ dimensional simplex $\triangle_0$, namely, a vertex, of $K$. The first set of degrees of freedom implies that $\tau \b \nu =0$ on $\partial K$ while the second set of degrees of freedom shows $\operatorname{div} \tau=0$. Then the third set of degrees of freedom proves that $\tau=0$. Next we shall prove that the sum of these degrees of freedom is equal to the dimension of the space $P_2^\ast(K, \mathbb{S})$. In fact the sum of the first set of degrees of freedom is \begin{equation*} \sum\limits_{\ell=0}^{n-1}C_{n+1}^{\ell+1}\frac{(n-\ell)(n+\ell+1)}{2}C_{n}^\ell, \end{equation*} we refer interested readers to \cite[Theorem 2.1]{Hu2014} for a detailed proof of the numbers of degrees of freedom in the first set. By the Chu-Vandermonde combinatorial identity \eqref{van} and its variant \eqref{varvan}, see more details from \cite{Hu2014}, \begin{equation*} \sum\limits_{\ell=0}^{n-1}C_{n+1}^{\ell+1}\frac{(n-\ell)(n+\ell+1)}{2}C_{n}^\ell=\frac{(2n+1)!}{n!(n+1)!}\frac{n(n+1)}{2}- \frac{(2n-1)!}{n!(n-1)!}\frac{n(n+1)}{2}. \end{equation*} Hence the desired result follows from \eqref{eq3.4}, and the sum of the second and third sets of degrees of freedom.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement:
Let $v_h\in V_{k,h}$. By the stability of the continuous formulation, cf. \cite{Arnold-Winther-conforming} for two dimensional case, there is a $	au \in H^1(\Omega; \mathbb{S})$ such that, \a{ \operatorname{div}	au=v_h \quad \hbox{m and } \quad \|	au\|_{1}\le C\|v_h\|_{0}. } In this paper, we only consider the domain such that the above stability holds. We refer interested authors to \cite{GiraultRaviart1986} for the classical result which states it is true for Lipschitz domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$; see \cite{Duran2001} for more refined results. First let $I_h$ be a Scott-Zhang \cite{Scott-Zhang} interpolation operator such that  egin{equation} \|	au-I_h	au\|_0+h\|
abla I_h	au\|_0\leq Ch\|
abla	au\|_0. \end{equation} These enriched bubble functions in $\sum\limits_{F}\mathbb{B}_F^1$ on the $n-1$ dimensional simplices $F$ allow for defining a correction $\delta_h\in \sum\limits_{F}\mathbb{B}_F^1$ such that  egin{equation} \int_{F} \delta_h
u \cdot p d   s=\int_{F} (	au-I_h	au)
u\cdot p d  s	ext{ for any } p\in R(K)|_{F}. \end{equation} Finally we take  egin{equation} 	au_h=I_h	au+\delta_h. \end{equation} We get a partial-divergence matching property of $	au_h$: for any $p\in R(K)$, as the symmetric gradient $\epsilon( p)=0$, \a{ \int_K (\operatorname{div}	au_h-v_h) \cdot p \, d  x & = \int_K (\operatorname{div}	au_h-\operatorname{div} 	au) \cdot p \, d  x\ & = \int_{\partial K} (	au_h-	au)
u\cdot p\, d  s =0.} The stability estimate follows from \eqref{eq3.9} and the definition of the correction $\delta_h$.
nodes.statement_short: Take continuous right inverse tau, Scott-Zhang interpolate, and correct with face bubbles so normal moments against rigid motions match.

nodes.name: Extension of Lemma 4.2 to k=n
nodes.statement: A modification of the above proof applies for the case where $k=n$. In fact, the bubble functions in the spaces $\widetilde \Sigma_{k,h}$ and $\sum\limits_{F}\mathbb{B}_F^2$ on the $n-1$ dimensional simplices $F$ are able to control the constant subspace of $R(K)$ and its orthogonal complement, respectively.

nodes.statement: For the discrete problem (\ref{DP}), the K-ellipticity \eqref{below} and the discrete B-B condition \eqref{inf-sup} hold uniformly. Consequently, the discrete mixed problem \eqref{DP} has a unique solution $(\sigma_h,~u_h)\in\Sigma_{k,h}^+\times V_{k,h}$.
conclusions: the K-ellipticity \eqref{below}     and the discrete B-B  condition \eqref{inf-sup} hold uniformly.
the discrete      mixed problem \eqref{DP} has a unique solution          $(\sigma_h,~u_h)\in\Sigma_{k,h}^+\times V_{k,h}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: The K-ellipticity immediately follows from the fact that $\operatorname{div} \Sigma_{k,h}^+ \subset V_{k,h}$. To prove the discrete B-B condition \eqref{inf-sup}, for any $v_h\in V_{k,h}$, it follows from Lemma \ref{lemma1} and Remark \ref{remark4.1} that there exists a $\tau_{1}\in \Sigma_{k,h}^+$ such that, for any polynomial $p\in R(K)$, \begin{equation} \int_K (\operatorname{div}\tau_1-v_h) \cdot pd\b x=0 \quad \hbox{\rm and } \quad \|\tau_1\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\leq C\|v_h\|_{0}. \end{equation} Then it follows from Lemma \ref{lemma2.3} that there is a $\tau_2\in\Sigma_{k, h}$ such that $\tau_2|_K \in \Sigma_{K, k, b}$ and \begin{equation} \operatorname{div}\tau_2 = v_h-\operatorname{div}\tau_1, \|\tau_2\|_0=\min\{\|\tau\|_0, \operatorname{div}\tau=v_h-\operatorname{div}\tau_1, \tau\in \Sigma_{K, k, b} \} \end{equation} It follows from the definition of $\tau_2$ that $\|\operatorname{div} \tau_2\|_0$ defines a norm for it. Then, a scaling argument proves \begin{equation} \|\tau_2 \|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\leq C\|\operatorname{div}\tau_1-v_h\|_{0}. \end{equation} Let $\tau=\tau_1+\tau_2$. This implies that \begin{equation} \operatorname{div}\tau=v_h \text{ and } \|\tau\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\leq C\|v_h\|_{0}, \end{equation} this proves the discrete B-B condition \eqref{inf-sup}.
nodes.statement_short: K-ellipticity from div inclusion; inf-sup by tau_1 from Lemma 4.2 plus element bubble tau_2 from Lemma 2.3 with scaling bound.

Then, for $2\leq k\leq n$, \an{ \lab{t1} \|\sigma-\sigma_h\|_{H({\rm div})} + \|u-u_h\|_{0}&\le Ch^k(\|\sigma\|_{k+1}+\|u\|_{k}). }

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement: The stability of the elements and the standard theory of mixed finite element methods \cite{Brezzi, Brezzi-Fortin} give the following quasioptimal error estimate immediately \an{ \|\sigma-\sigma_h\|_{H({\rm div})}+\|u-u_h\|_{0}\leq C \inf\limits_{\tau_h\in\Sigma_{k,h}^+,v_h\in V_{k,h}}\left(\|\sigma-\tau_h\|_{H({\rm div})}+\|u-v_h\|_{0}\right).} Let $P_h$ denote the local $L^2$ projection operator, or element-wise interpolation operator, from $V$ to $V_{k,h}$, satisfying the error estimate \an{ \|v-P_hv\|_{0}\leq Ch^k\|v\|_{k} \text{ for any }v\in H^k(\Omega; \mathbb{R}^n). } Choosing $\tau_h=I_h\sigma\in \Sigma_{k,h}$ where $I_h$ is defined in \eqref{eq3.9} as $I_h$ preserves symmetric $P_k$ functions locally, \an{ \lab{p-err2} \|\sigma -\tau_h\|_{0} + h |\sigma -\tau_h|_{H(\operatorname{div})} \le Ch^{k+1} \|\sigma\|_{k+1}. } Let $v_h= P_h v$ and $\tau_h=I_h\sigma$ in (\ref{theorem-err1}), by (\ref{proj-error}) and \eqref{p-err2}, we obtain \eqref{t1}.
nodes.statement_short: Quasi-optimality from stability (Brezzi theory), then approximation by L^2 projection and Scott-Zhang interpolation.

nodes.statement: To prove an optimal error estimate for the stress in the $L^2$ norm, we can follow the idea from \cite{Stenberg-1} to use a mesh dependent norm technique. In particular, this will lead to $$ \|\sigma-\sigma_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq Ch^{k+1}|\sigma|_{H^{k+1}(\Omega)}. $$

nodes.name: Numerical test: 2D pure displacement problem
nodes.statement:
We compute a 2D pure displacement problem  on the unit square $\Omega=[0,1]^2$
     with a homogeneous boundary condition
         that $u\equiv 0$ on $\partial\Omega$.
In the computation, we let the compliance tensor in \eqref{eqn1}
   \a{
      A \sigma &= \frac 1{2\mu} \left(
       \sigma - \frac{\lambda}{2\mu + n \lambda} \operatorname{tr}(\sigma)
        \delta \right), \quad n=2,  }
  where $\delta=\p{1 &0\\0&1}$, and $\mu=1/2$ and $\lambda=1$ are the
    Lam\'e constants.
Let  the  exact solution be
   \e{\lab{e-2}   u= \p{ e^{x-y}x (1-x) y (1-y)\\
    \sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y)}. }
The true stress function $\sigma$
     and the load function $f$ are defined by the equations in
    \eqref{eqn1},   for the given  solution $u$.
nodes.statement_short: Unit-square elasticity test with mu=1/2, lambda=1 and a smooth exact displacement.

nodes.name: Observed optimal convergence for the k=2 element
nodes.statement:
We use the bubble enriched $P_2$ symmetric stress finite element with
   $P_1$ discontinuous displacement finite element, $k=2$ in \eqref{Vh} and in
    \eqref{Sh-plus}, and $k=2$ in \eqref{Sh}.
That is, 3 $P_3$ bubbles are enriched each edge.
In Table \ref{b-2}, the errors and the convergence order
   in various norms are listed  for the true solution \eqref{e-2}.
The optimal order of convergence is observed  for both displacement and stress,
  see Table \ref{b-2}, as shown in the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: With the 2D k=2 element, optimal convergence orders are observed for displacement and stress.

nodes.name: Comparison with the Arnold-Winther element
nodes.statement:
As a comparison,  we also test   the Arnold--Winther element from \cite{Arnold-Winther-conforming}, which  has a same degree of freedom as ours, 21, on each  element.
But the displacement in that element
   is approximated by the rigid-motion space only,
   instead of the full $P_1$ space, i.e., 3 dof vs 6 dof on each triangle. The total degrees of freedom for the stress for the new element are $3|\mathbb{V}|+3|\mathbb{E}|+3|\mathbb{K}|$, where    $|\mathbb{V}|$, $|\mathbb{E}|$, and $|\mathbb{K}|$ are the numbers of vertices, edges and elements of $\mathcal{T}_h$, respectively, while those for the Arnold--Winther element are $3|\mathbb{V}|+4|\mathbb{E}|$.  Since the
       three bubble functions on each element can be easily condensed,  these two elements almost have  the same complexity for solving.
The errors and the orders of convergence are listed in Table \ref{b-3}.
Because the new element uses the full $P_1$ displacement space, the order of
convergence is one higher than that of the Arnold--Winther element.
Also as the new element includes the full $P_2$ stress space, the order of
  convergence of stress is one order higher, see  the data in Tables \ref{b-2} and \ref{b-3}.
nodes.statement_short: Same DOF count as Arnold-Winther but one order higher convergence, due to the full P_1 displacement and P_2 stress.
